title: Arcade vs HowdyGo vs Storylane Demo Suite (2026)
summary: Arcade vs HowdyGo vs Storylane Demo Suite: compare capture format, 2026 pricing, AI video vs HTML demos, and which interactive demo tool fits your team.
body_markdown:
Most "arcade vs howdygo" pages you will find are either a vendor landing page or a thin spec chart, and none of them account for what actually changed this year. Here is my thesis, and I will defend it: for most go-to-market teams in 2026, the right choice comes down to one question the SERP keeps burying, which is what your demos are made of.


Arcade stitches screenshots and, increasingly, AI video. HowdyGo captures your real HTML. Pick the format that survives your product roadmap, and the rest of the decision gets easy.


Full disclosure up top so you can weigh everything I say: I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and we build in this category. I have kept the head-to-head honest, named where each tool beats us, and put our own section where it belongs rather than at the top.


If you only want the verdict, jump to the decision block. If you want to understand why the format question matters more than price, read on.


The buyers I talk to do not fail at picking a tool. They fail at maintenance. The demo looks great on day one and quietly breaks on day forty when the product ships a new screen, and that is the lens I want you to keep as we go through capture format, pricing, and workflow.


## Arcade vs HowdyGo at a glance


Both tools sell the same promise: build an interactive product demo without engineering, then embed or share it. The difference is what they capture and who they are priced for.


HowdyGo leans into real HTML capture on a flat, unlimited-user plan. Arcade leans into fast screenshot-and-video tours with per-seat pricing and a free entry point.


Here is the fast version before we go deep. If you are still assembling the rest of[your sales tech stack](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tools-to-build-the-best-sales-tech-stack) , treat this table as a shortlist, not a verdict.


Dimension Arcade HowdyGo Storylane Demo Suite


Capture format Screenshots + hotspots, plus AI video Real HTML/CSS capture Both screenshot and HTML capture, plus video


Starting price Free plan; Pro ~$32/user/mo $159/mo flat, unlimited users Sits between the two on price


Free plan Yes No (14-day trial) Yes


Best for Fast screenshot and video tours, small teams Interactive HTML demos, team rollouts Teams that want both formats in one tool


Rating ~4.7/5 ~4.8-5.0/5 Strong across G2 and G2 momentum


The ratings are directional and move over time, so weight them lightly. What does not move is the capture-format decision, which is where nearly every real-world regret comes from, so that is the next section.


One more framing note before you read the table: Arcade optimizes for how fast and polished a demo looks, while HowdyGo optimizes for how real it behaves and how many people can publish without extra cost. Neither optimization is wrong, but they pull in different directions, and the table above reads very differently depending on which one matches your team.


## The core difference: capture format


Everything else is downstream of this. Arcade records your screen as a sequence of screenshots stitched together with hotspots and, in its newer product, generated video. HowdyGo captures the actual HTML and CSS of your app, so form fields, dropdowns and transitions behave like the live product inside the demo.


> **Definition:** An interactive demo tool creates a clickable, self-guided replica of your software that a prospect can explore on their own, embedded on a website, sent in an email, or shared as a link, without spinning up a real environment or booking a live call.


That definition splits cleanly along format. A screenshot tour is faster to make and forgiving to edit, but it is a picture of your product, not your product. An HTML capture feels real and handles complex flows, but it is heavier to build and more sensitive to how your front end is coded.


> Callout: the format you choose is the format you maintain. Screenshot tours are easy to spin up but re-recorded when the UI moves. HTML captures survive small UI changes better but demand more setup up front.


This is exactly why teams end up wanting[self-serve interactive demos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-requests) that route buyers to the product without a rep. The tool that does that well for you depends on how often your UI changes and how interactive the flow needs to feel.


## What changed with Arcade in 2026


This is the part most comparison pages get wrong, and it is the single biggest reason to distrust anything written before this year. Arcade has repositioned around video and AI creation first, with its Creator Studio and Avery AI assistant front and center. The classic interactive-demo capabilities did not disappear, but several moved up the pricing ladder.


Specifically, HTML capture, Demo Collections, custom share links, offline access and the Salesforce integration are now gated to Arcade's Enterprise tier. If your evaluation assumed HTML demos came standard with Arcade, that assumption is out of date, and it changes the pricing math in the next section considerably.


Arcade capability Before 2026 In 2026


HTML capture Available on standard tiers Enterprise only


Demo Collections Standard Enterprise only


Custom share links Standard Enterprise only


Salesforce integration Standard Enterprise only


Product focus Interactive demos first Video and AI creation first (Creator Studio, Avery AI)


The practical effect is a fork. If you want Arcade purely for quick screenshot-and-video walkthroughs, the self-serve tiers are still a strong, cheap option. If you specifically wanted Arcade for interactive HTML demos, you are now looking at an Enterprise conversation with a seat minimum, which puts it in a very different bracket than HowdyGo's flat plan.


For teams leaning into the video angle of the pivot, our own take on[product demo and explainer videos](https://www.storylane.io/blog/saas-product-demo-and-explainer-videos) covers where video helps and where it quietly underperforms an interactive tour.


## Feature-by-feature comparison


Read this table for capability, then read the pricing section for what each capability costs, because in 2026 those are no longer the same question. A feature Arcade technically has is not a feature you necessarily get on the plan you can afford.


Feature Arcade HowdyGo Storylane Demo Suite


Capture format Screenshots + video HTML/CSS capture Screenshots + HTML capture


Edit without re-recording Limited, re-record screens Yes, no-code HTML editor Yes


Animations and transitions Strong, video-based Native app transitions Yes


Sandbox / live-feel demos Screenshot simulation Real interactive HTML Yes, Sandbox Demos


Branching / personalization Yes Yes Yes


Analytics Native on higher tiers Native analytics on Pro Yes


CRM integrations Salesforce on Enterprise CRM integrations on Pro Yes


In-app tours Yes Yes Yes


Video export Strong Limited Yes


AI features Avery AI, Creator Studio Lighter AI tooling Lily AI


Two rows deserve a caveat. Arcade's HTML capture is real and good, but it now lives on Enterprise, so a self-serve buyer effectively does not have it. HowdyGo's video story is thinner than Arcade's, so if polished narrated video is your primary format, that gap is real and worth weighing honestly against everything else.


The "edit without re-recording" row is the one I would stare at longest, because it is the feature you will exercise most after launch. HowdyGo's no-code editor lets you duplicate a demo, re-text it and blur data without capturing the screen again, which is a genuinely different maintenance model than Arcade's screenshot-and-hotspot approach.


Analytics and CRM integrations also cluster on paid tiers for both tools, so treat the free or entry plans as a way to test capture quality, not as the plan you will actually run a team on. Read the table as capability first, then let the pricing section tell you what each row really costs on the plan you can afford.


## Pricing compared


Pricing is where the 2026 shift bites hardest, so let me lay out the tiers plainly and then explain the crossover. The models are structurally different: Arcade charges per seat, HowdyGo charges a flat rate for unlimited users.


Plan Arcade HowdyGo


Free Free plan None (14-day trial)


Entry paid Pro ~$32/user/mo, single seat Starter $159/mo flat, unlimited users


Mid tier Growth ~$42.50/user/mo, up to 10 users Pro $399/mo, analytics, CRM, custom domains


HTML capture Enterprise, custom, ~10-seat minimum Included on every plan


Add-ons Not applicable Sandbox add-on ~$99/mo


The crossover math is simple once you see it. HowdyGo's Starter is a flat $159 per month for unlimited users with HTML capture included on every plan, so a five-person team pays the same as one person. Arcade's Growth tier at roughly $42.50 per user for up to ten users can beat that for a two or three-person team, but scale the seats and the flat plan wins, and if you need HTML you are comparing HowdyGo's $159 against Arcade Enterprise, which is a different order of magnitude.


Do not copy any of these numbers into a board deck without checking each vendor's live pricing page, because the figures across the SERP genuinely conflict and both vendors adjust tiers. Verify, then decide. What rarely changes is the shape: per-seat rewards small teams and punishes rollouts, flat-rate does the opposite.


## Demo creation speed and workflow


Speed and interactivity trade off against each other, and the pack of buyers I hear from feel this immediately. Arcade's screenshot tours come together fast, often in the five-to-fifteen-minute range for a straightforward flow. HowdyGo's HTML capture takes longer up front, closer to fifteen-to-thirty minutes, because you are capturing and cleaning real markup rather than snapping frames.


Here is the workflow difference as a sequence, because "faster" is meaningless without saying faster at what:


1. Capture: Arcade records your screen; HowdyGo captures the live DOM of the page.
2. Clean up: Arcade tours need hotspot placement; HowdyGo demos need data blurred and text edited in a no-code editor.
3. Personalize: both let you swap text and images per prospect, but HTML capture lets a viewer actually interact with fields.
4. Ship: both give you an embed and a shareable link.


The speed argument matters most for volume. One buyer described the payoff of a short interactive demo as a follow-up that actually gets watched, which is worth more than a fast build you send and never hear about again.


- "For me being in sales for the past, the frustrating types of sales calls is the person who shows up on the website, they read the headlines in the value proposition and they're not entirely sure, but they go ahead and just book a call and take up time on your calendar. But it's not a good fit for them and it ends up being a demo call to nowhere." - \[marketing lead, software\]


That quote is the real speed argument. Fast demo creation only pays off if the demo does qualification work before a human spends a calendar slot on it.


## Editing and maintenance when your product changes


This is the section I would read first if I were buying, because it is the pain that actually costs money over a year. Every demo tool looks equal in a trial. They diverge the first time your product ships a redesign and someone has to fix forty demos.


- "It's hard to keep up. It's always been hard, but it's even harder now \[with how quickly we're shipping product\]." - \[product/brand marketing lead, software\]


That is the whole game. A product manager put the underlying data problem the same way, and it is why "just re-record it" is not a real answer at scale.


- "The problem we have today is like our demo environments. It's hard to keep like fresh data, fresh test data and all those things in there." - \[product manager, software\]


Here is a worked example to make the maintenance cost concrete. Say you keep 30 demos live and your product ships a UI change to a core screen once a quarter.


With a screenshot tour, a changed screen means re-recording every affected demo, so if 10 of your 30 demos touch that screen and each takes 20 minutes to rebuild, that is roughly 3.3 hours of rework per quarter, about 13 hours a year, per person who owns demos. With HowdyGo's no-code HTML editor you often duplicate, re-text and re-blur rather than rebuild, which cuts the per-demo fix meaningfully when the change is textual rather than structural.


Neither tool makes maintenance free, and a genuine structural redesign forces rework on both, so the honest claim is smaller and more durable: HTML capture shortens routine, text-level maintenance, and screenshots win only when the demo never has to change.


## Arcade vs HowdyGo: which should you choose?


No tool wins this outright, so match the tool to your constraints rather than to a feature count. Here is how I would decide.


**Choose Arcade if:**


- Your primary format is screenshot tours or narrated video, not deep interactivity.
- You have a small team and per-seat pricing on the self-serve tiers is cheaper than a flat plan for you.
- You want the fastest possible time from screen recording to shareable tour.
- You do not need HTML capture, Collections or Salesforce, or you are ready for an Enterprise contract to get them.


**Choose HowdyGo if:**


- You need real HTML interactivity where fields and dropdowns work.
- You will roll demos out to many users and want unlimited-seat flat pricing.
- Hands-on founder support from a small team appeals to you more than a large vendor.
- Your demos change often at the text and data level and you want to edit without re-recording.


If neither fits cleanly, that is a signal to look at[other interactive demo alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/consensus-alternatives) before you commit, because a forced fit here is expensive to unwind later.


## Where Storylane Demo Suite fits


Full disclosure: this is us, so read it with the appropriate skepticism. I am including Storylane because the format-first framing above naturally raises the question of whether you have to choose screenshot-or-HTML at all, and our whole design bet is that you should not have to.


Quick product note so the comparison is fair: Storylane's Demo Suite is the product that competes head-to-head with Arcade and HowdyGo, while Storylane Demo Suite is our separate AI agent for inbound website conversion, so Demo Suite is the right column to weigh here.


Storylane's Demo Suite supports both screenshot capture and HTML capture, plus video and an AI assistant (Lily), and on price we sit between Arcade's self-serve tiers and an enterprise platform rather than at either extreme. The mechanism is straightforward: you capture in whichever format a given demo needs, keep them in Demo Hubs, and route engaged viewers to a next step instead of leaving them stranded at the end of a tour. That last part matters because buyers consistently ask for a built-in path from self-serve exploration to talking to a human.


Where we do not fit: if you want the absolute cheapest single-seat screenshot tool, Arcade's free and Pro tiers undercut us, and if you want one founder personally in your Slack, HowdyGo's size is a real advantage we cannot match. I would rather you know that now than churn later. If you want the longer version, here is[how Storylane compares to other demo tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/storylane-alternatives) .


**Choose Storylane Demo Suite if:**


- You want both screenshot capture and HTML capture in one tool, so you do not have to choose a single format.
- You are scaling demos to multiple users and need flat-rate, predictable pricing without per-seat surprises.
- Demo Hubs let you group demos into one destination, routing engaged buyers to a next step rather than leaving them stranded.
- Sandbox Demos give buyers a live-feeling interactive environment without engineering ownership.
- A free trial matters: start without a sales conversation and build your first demo today.


## Use-case fit by team and company stage


Tool choice is not just format and price, it is who is using it and what job the demo does, so map it to your stage and team before you buy. The self-serve tiers that suit a Seed team break down when a Growth-stage org needs ten people publishing governed demos.


Stage and team Likely best fit Why


Seed / Series A, marketing embeds Arcade self-serve Free or cheap entry, fast screenshot tours


Growth, 1:1 sales leave-behinds HowdyGo Flat pricing across many reps, interactive feel


Growth, CS onboarding HowdyGo Editable HTML survives frequent UI changes


Enterprise, partner enablement Arcade Enterprise or a fuller platform Governance, Collections, deeper integrations


Any stage, both formats needed Storylane Demo Suite Screenshot and HTML capture in one tool


A few patterns from the field are worth calling out. Marketing teams embedding demos on the homepage care most about capture speed and how the demo looks, while sales teams care most about the leave-behind: a short interactive demo sent after a discovery call, highlighting exactly what was discussed, instead of a long recording nobody opens.


Presales and CS teams care most about maintenance, because they own the demos long enough to feel every product change. If you are mapping this across a portfolio of pages, our[Tourial alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tourial-alternatives) breakdown covers the embed-heavy end of that spectrum in more detail.


The buyers with the largest teams described the goal as leverage across a whole portfolio, and that is the stage-based tell: once you need many people producing personalized demos, flat pricing and reusable capture beat a cheap per-seat plan every time.


- "So just helping the team get leverage across our portfolio will be critical... making it really easy for the PMMs to either scrape the UI, gather the screenshots, produce highly personalized demos by industry type by solution set. So personalization will be key." - \[product/brand marketing lead, software\]


## FAQ


**Is Arcade or HowdyGo cheaper?**


It depends entirely on team size and whether you need HTML. For a one-to-three-person team using screenshot tours, Arcade's per-seat self-serve tiers are usually cheaper. For a larger team, HowdyGo's flat $159 per month for unlimited users typically wins, and if you need HTML from Arcade you are comparing against Enterprise, which is far more expensive than HowdyGo's flat plan.


**Does HowdyGo have a free plan?**


No. HowdyGo does not offer a permanent free plan; it runs a 14-day trial and then starts at a flat $159 per month on Starter, with HTML capture included on every paid plan and unlimited users. Arcade, by contrast, does offer a free tier, which is often the deciding factor for very small teams testing the category.


**Does Arcade still do HTML demos?**


Yes, but not on the plans most people start with. As of Arcade's 2026 changes, HTML capture along with Demo Collections, custom share links and the Salesforce integration moved to the Enterprise tier. If interactive HTML is your reason for choosing Arcade, budget for an Enterprise contract rather than a self-serve seat.


**Which is better for email embeds?**


Both generate shareable links and embeds, so either works for email. Arcade's screenshot-and-video tours tend to load fast and look polished in an email context, while HowdyGo's HTML demos give a more interactive click-through once the prospect opens them. Choose based on whether you want a quick visual teaser or a genuine hands-on click.


**Can these replace enterprise demo platforms?**


For most website, marketing and mid-market sales use cases, yes, and at a fraction of the cost of platforms aimed at heavy sales-engineering enablement. Where they stop is deep, data-rich sandbox environments and governance that large enterprises require, at which point a fuller platform earns its price. Match the tool to the job rather than over-buying.
